655.t: Getting the Donald Fagen Rock and Soul Revue gig
655.s: Fagen heard him at Elaine's with Frank Vignola. Ascione sent R&B demos and joined the Rock and Soul Revue with Doctor John and Phoebe Snow.
655.q: Yeah, very cool. I did a gig at a place on 89th Street in New York called Elaine’s, that’s some posh upper east side place. Frank Vignola, great guitarist, I work a lot with him, we’re great friends and do a lot of musical business work together. We were doing a gig, a trio or quartet at Elaine’s.…

655.t: First Fagen show at the Lone Star; Noel Redding trio
655.s: The first Rock and Soul Revue show in New York, then a recent Hendrix-tune trio with Noel Redding and Eric Schenkman. He says labels are just for talking about music.
655.q: Yeah, the first show was in New York at the old Lone Star, the one with the iguana outside. And it was a real rush, it really was. That was the first experience I had like the whole group coming together and saying a prayer before going out in front of the — you know it was real hype type stuff.…

656.t: Maynard's stamina; the 1981 phone call from Dave Brubeck
656.s: After Maynard, Florida and a fusion band, Dave Brubeck phoned him for an audition, having noted his Sugar Bush flute solo of 1977.
656.q: He’s very into his yoga and his thing that he does that way and all that stuff. And he’s a road rat. Road rats tend to be able to deal with the road and the turmoils and the physical stresses and that kind of stuff. You know I’m a heavy guy and everything else and our schedule with Dave is busy as…

656.t: Auditioning with Brubeck, Joe Morello and Eugene Wright
656.s: At the audition with the original quartet he played new tunes and Kathy's Waltz, emulating Paul Desmond.
656.q: So I walk into the original quartet, which is like a dream, I mean I had memorized all those Desmond things and all that stuff. So I walked in and had done my homework on the new tunes. But I didn’t have to do my homework on the old tunes because I already knew them. So Dave says, “Well what do you…

508.t: The Grateful Dead's musicianship and under-the-radar concerts
508.s: He admires the Dead as musicians who called tunes on stage, sold out arenas without media and had no celebrity row.
508.ch: Radio, acting and playing outside jazz
508.q: I loved it. That was fun. I didn’t…. I had not heard a Dead song since the seventies. For a long time that thing functioned completely under the radar, which to me is the best possible world to be in. Cause they were actually musicians, and they were fans of the music that they listened to. Phil…

508.t: Sitting in with the Grateful Dead and playing Dark Star
508.s: He sat in on Eyes of the World, was asked to stay for the second set, and played Dark Star for a roaring crowd.
508.ch: Radio, acting and playing outside jazz
508.q: So they bring me up on the last tune of the first set, of course. “Thanks for playing. Get the fuck out of here.” (laughs) It makes perfect sense. So, I played the tune. And it was “Eyes of the World” or “Bird Song,” one of the two. I can’t remember which one it was. I think it was “Eyes.” And,…

539.t: After Atlantic: Warner Brothers, the Midler fallout and Leon Redbone
539.s: Dorn left Atlantic for Warner Brothers briefly. He was shaken by being thrown off the first Bette Midler album, then worked with Asleep at the Wheel, Don McLean and Leon Redbone.
539.q: Rahsaan and I went to Warner Brothers for a minute, Fathead was at Warner Brothers for a minute. But that was kind of it. I went off into another thing. I had had a really bad experience making that first Bette Midler record. They threw me off it and then the cuts that I made became the hits and…

657.s: Relationship began opening for DMB with Soulive; sitting in with LeRoi Moore and Jeff Coffin.
657.q: Great, yeah. It was amazing. And I was good friends. Well you know our relationship with them started with Soulive. We went on tour opening up for them, like we did this southern tour and then I became friends with LeRoi, the saxophone player who passed away, and so we kind of just had a…

658.s: Meeting Bob Weir through a Satchel Paige musical, sitting in at Madison Square Garden, Jerry Garcia, and his jazz album of Dead music.
658.q: Oh well, you know, God, first of all Bob Weir is really a good friend of mine. And the way we met was through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams. They asked me to be part of this — of writing the music for a musical about Satchel Paige. And so we began to collaborate, Taj Mahal, Bob Weir and myself,…

659.t: Working with Aretha Franklin and Steely Dan
659.s: He loved Aretha but found her personal side hard, found Steely Dan demanding but fine, and says he does the job and leaves.
659.q: To me it was great years. I had more problems than a barrel of monkeys on the personal side but that’s what I had to learn to live with. Aretha is one of the best, one of the best performers in the world. Not great with business and personal life she’s had all kinds of problems. It affected me and…

660.t: The Willow Weep for Me, Satisfaction and Beer Barrel Polka medley
660.s: Ries explains how the medley arose, with Al's accordion and his memory of playing polkas in his dad's band.
660.q: Wow. And I did not plan that in any way it just — oh my God well I realized ‘cause we were going to go until ten o’clock. And I looked at my watch and it was like oh so maybe we were in “Willow Weep for Me” at like ten to ten because I didn’t want to go too much past that or whatever, and I thought…

661.t: Catch a Rising Star and the Donald Fagen band
661.s: Singing between comics led to Donald Fagen's band and Steely Dan touring, and calls from famous people.
661.q: his shows so he started doing HBO shows, so I was called to do that as a result of doing demos for Bob Stein, who is his musical director. So like all these things kind of started happening and then I started sitting in in bands in New York. And then I was doing weddings at the same time, meeting…
